1 CCMP general information 
1.1  CCMP description  
The Project is structured as a 30-year REDD+ project starting officially on July 1, 2017 ending 
on June 30, 2022 that has the total participation of all 12,128 members of the community. 
The project ensures environmental Sustainability and mitigate the existing threats posed by 
the main agents and drivers of deforestation. 
The Project is located in far southwest region of the state of Para.  The project has a total 
of 354,132.01 hectares. After an analysis of agents and causes of deforestation, a leakage 
belt of a buffer project area of 2 km was defined. This leakage area includes 96,317.1 ha of 
forest area. The Project is structured as a 30 -year REDD project starting officially on July 1, 
2017 ending on June 30, 2047 that has the total participation of all of the community. The 
project foresees the reduction of emissions of 16,985,381 tCO2e during the 30 years of its 
useful life, that is, an average of 641,198 tCO2e per year. 
For this purpose, the implementation of a project Reduction of Emissions due to Deforesta-
tion, is proposed. This will allow providing payments for emission reductions, considered an 
ecosystem service of the forests that the communities preserve through the care of the 
forests. 
Therefore, the collective territories linked to the project seek, through their territorial au-
tonomy, to carry out conservation processes that preserve their cultural identity and pro-
mote the protection of the biodiversity and environmental wealth of their  territory. Char-
acteristics directly linked to the purpose of  REDD+ projects, with the desired sustainable 
and sustainable local development, as well as to reduce emissions generated due to defor-
estation. 
The Indigenous people as proponents of the project, where the states of Para and Mato 
Grosso meet, is a transition zone where the Amazon biome switch to the Cerrado (bush 
land) Biome to the south of the Amazon Biome in tropical humid forests in the municip ali-
ties.  Within the reserve of Munduruku there are over 300,000 hectares of natural savannah 
and poor soil locations where the forest does not grow. 
With the implementation of the Project, it is intended to comply with 8 of 17 SDG’s as can 
be seen listed in section 11 of the CCMP. 
Nevertheless, not all Sustainable Development Goals were met in the first monitoring pe-
riod of the project as numerous require funding from carbon credits beyond the financial 
means of the proponents to allow for the project to succeed in that area. 
The Project has been fully operational since July 1, 2017 with the goal is to prove out the 
economic feasibility of preserving the forest in regions that are  already heavily degraded, 
and where it is still considered socially acceptable to convert forest to agriculture.

The project corresponds to the Scope of Unplanned Emissions from deforestation, aiming 
to protect rainforests, which are expected to be deforested in the absence of Project.  The 
primary focus has been to reduce and eventually climate illegal logging.  As well as quantify 
the reduction in wood leaving the reserve. 
Likewise, the project proponents, since the start date, have led initiatives of an environ-
mental nature and climatic additionality with the technical and financial support of institu-
tional and governmental, which have in their jurisdiction of operation the territories of the 
proposing indigenous reservations. 
Sector: 14 – Agriculture, Forestry and other land use (AFOLU) 
Category: Reducing emissions from deforestation (REDD+) 
Project Type: Type 1 removes or reduces 10,000 or more tons of CO2e, in average per year 
GHG. 
In reserves, there are no avoided planned deforestation scopes. 
1.2  CCMP hold er information   
The project's proponent is the Munduruku indigenous people of the Munduruku Indigenous 
Territory, located in the state of Pará. It is a reserve of over 2,500,000 hectares with 34 
villages and 12,128 members among 2,400 families.  
The community has a cacique in each village as a leadership position, in addition to the AIP 
association, which represents all the Munduruku people and has the authority and right to 
exploit the credits. The social organization functions with the collaboration of the commu-
nity, through voting and meetings. In this way, decision making is carried out taking the 
position of the population into consideration. 
The indigenous population has the right of possession and usufruct guaranteed by the 1988 
Constitution of the Federative Republic of Brazil over the lands they occupy, thus possessing 
carbon rights.  
The Munduruku people in their role as proponents designate the company Indigenous Car-
bon LLC to assist in the execution of the carbon credit project, giving them the right to mon-
etize the credits on behalf of the community.  
Each of the following project proponents have the rights to withdraw GHG removals or GHG 
emission reduction Certificates as is listed in the contracts related to project set up.  How-
ever in order to withdraw they have to equally sign, as each person collec tively represents 
their people and the reserve. Thus, one individual person can’t withdraw without the con-
sent of everyone else.

1.3  Information from other CCMP institutional stakeholders  
FUNAI - The Fundação Nacional do Índio (Funai) 
FUNAI is a participant stakeholder because staff from this government agencies have par-
ticipated in social events, and they have observed events.  This makes them a relevant 
stakeholder. 
FUNAI is the official indigenous agency of the Brazilian State. Created by Law No. 5,371, of 
December 5, 1967, linked to the Ministry of Justice and Public Security, this is the main 
agency overseeing the Federal Government's indigenous policy. Its institu tional mission is 
to protect and promote the rights of the indigenous people in Brazil. 
It is the responsibility of FUNAI to provide studies of identification, delimitation, determi-
nation, demarcation, land regularization, and registration of lands traditionally occupied by 
indigenous people, in addition to monitoring and supervising indigeno us lands. FUNAI also 
coordinates and implements policies for the protection of isolated and newly recruited peo-
ple. 
Also, it’s still, their role to promote policies aimed at the sustainable development of indig-
enous populations.  In this field, FUNAI promotes actions of ethnic development, conserva-
tion, and recovery of the environment on indigenous territory, in additio n to acting not to 
control and mitigate possible environmental impacts resulting from external interference 
on indigenous lands. However, due to funding constraints, it is not always possible. 
It is also the responsibility of the agency to establish an inter-institutional articulation aimed 
between indigenous and non -indigenous people, and guarantee differentiated access to

FUNAI's action is guided by various principles, among which stands out or recognition of the 
social organization, costumes, languages, beliefs, and traditions of the two indigenous peo-
ple, seeking the full independence and self-determination of the indigenous people in Bra-
zil, contributing to the consolidation democratic and multi-ethnic state.

According to the start date of the project, the following actions implemented by the reser-
vations as proponents of the REDD+ project were recognized for the current monitoring 
period set forth in collaboration with different entities: 
The following actions defined by lines of action contribute to the objective of the project, 
being aimed at satisfying and strengthening environmental aspects and the well -being of 
the communities that are part of the project. Based on these considerations, it is recognized 
that the project begins on July 1, 2017 with the management and planning instruments for 
the territory formulated prior to this data in relation to security measures, and SDG 
measures be formulated after this date. 
The proponents, who hold the right to the land, have implemented projects, agreements 
and contracts executed within the project area (the data has been provided to the DOE), in 
association with public, private, and mixed entities, with different participation mechanisms 
depending on the capacities of the parties. These actions have ensured that climate addi-
tionality is achieved by reducing greenhouse gas emissions, framed by the United Nations 
Framework Commission on Climate Change (UNFCCC). In the first place, there is the formu-
lation of the cultural and environmental management plan for the Reserve, which the re-
serve implements and develops through the support of the local FUNAI office. With this, a 
recognition of t he problems related to the environmental aspect and quality of life. This 
defines certain actions that have contributed to the loss of habitats, such as the extraction 
of wood with chainsaws, crops for illicit use, hunting, fishing, and poor garbage manage-
ment. With this exercise, certain agreements were proposed between the inhabitants of 
the reservation and five projects were prioritized to improve the situation that they had 
identified at the time. Under the guidelines given by this instrument, activities were devel-
oped to comply with the agreements and the prioritized projects, among these were per-
formed. 
Description of the activities to reduce deforestation of the monitoring plan 
The project has overcome several compliance and other safeguards by restricting involve-
ment by outside groups.  As can be seen in the project, the owner of the project are the 
indigenous, by having the indigenous as the managers and decision makers the project is 
able to have the safeguards in place the protect their cultu re. This process was carried out 
through the identification of socio-environmental aspects of the communities that required 
decisive actions for the efficiency of the project. This identification was validated through a 
process of joint construction with t he communities of the activities to be carried out and 
the technologies to be applied within the framework of the project. Seeking, on the one 
hand, to guarantee the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions greenhouse, and on the 
other hand, leave the capacities installed in the communities so that the results of the pro-
ject are maintained over time. In summary, the lines of action are presented.

Figure 1. Lines of action of the project 
 
As it can be seen in the figure above, there are some fundamental aspects consigned in the 
transversal lines of action, which seek to strengthen the indigenous reservations in funda-
mental elements for the management of the territory and the activities of t he REDD+ pro-
ject. 
Among the defined lines, some transversal ones were proposed, which from the experience 
of the team and the project structuring, have been identified as important in the rural areas 
of the country, since they contribute with aspects that have been identifi ed as common 
needs. 
Among these lines, there is institutional strengthening and governance, where the recovery 
of culture, traditions and in general of all the ancestral knowledge of the communities is 
sought, in the first place, highlighting traditional dances and rites. Secondly, the recovery of 
governance is intended, understood as decision -making based on information. This is, in a 
timely and participatory manner, in order to guarantee management of the territory in ac-
cordance with the vision of the reservations, under criteria of environmental and social sus-
tainability. This through the construction of the corresponding planning instruments, the 
training of leaders and the construction of meeting spaces. 
Among these are also the reforestation and monitoring lines that seek to generate coverage 
recovery and monitoring processes and their behavior. This through participatory processes 
that allow the training of communities, and their subsequent incorporation into activities  
such as the construction of nurseries, planting processes of species that have been 


--- Page 15 ---
 
Rio Crepori REDD+ Project – Version 3.0 
 
Monitoring Report for CCMP in the Land Use Sector  
  15 
 
identified by the communities, and subsequently, guarantee active participation in matters 
corresponding to the follow-up, monitoring, and control of these lines. 
There are also the health and education lines, focused, on the one hand, on strengthening 
the communities in technical aspects, on guaranteeing access to higher education, and es-
pecially, the provision of health services that are adapted to the physical an d cultural con-
ditions of the communities. 
However, in the joint work with the communities, aspects that require attention and activ-
ities focused on strengthening them were identified. Thus, the need to strengthen produc-
tion for self-consumption, characteristic of the reservations, was recognized, which is why 
special attention is sought drop irrigation for staple food crops.  In accordance with this, the 
need to diversify agricultural products was determined, for which a line focused on non -
conventional agroforestry products was prioritized, seekin g the possibility of generating 
self-sustaining food and to the same extent developing practices that go in agreement with 
the REDD+ project. 
This same analysis was carried for creating systems in line with the project for food products 
to sell. The indigenous people came up with a plan to create a Brazil Nut export business, 
and have set up the industry, but do not, as of yet have financial means to set up the indus-
try.  The industry is to help create employment as well as create a product that will bring in 
income. 
Lastly, there are the activities focused on the acquisition and improvement of the infrastruc-
ture of the indigenous reservation. Among these activities, fundamental aspects for the 
communities were recognized, which contribute to strengthening the culture,  knowledge, 
and connectivity of the territories with the rest of the country. Therefore, the acquisition 
and improvement of community infrastructure such as health clinics, schools, housing for 
teachers to come to schools, houses for medical staff, general  meeting areas. This is all in-
cluded in the project, and some activities have already been completed since the start date 
of the project and other activities are underway as well as new infrastructure planned in 
the future.  See section 11 SDG goals for all activities planned. 
The Brazil's presentation of a Forest Reference Emissions Level (FREL), submitted to be ap-
plied for emission reduction results achieved in the Amazonia biome in the period results -
based payments under the UNFCCC, was used. Due to the project area is locate d in this 
biome, so a procedure of clipping with FREL data base (Terrabrasilis, INPE and Prodes) in a 
GIS software was carried out to get the baseline information at a watershed scale as it is 
suggested in the Methodology M/UT-REDD+ V 1.3.1. This same data base was also consid-
ered to get the information of the deforested areas in the project zone and monitoring pe-
riod (2017-2022).  Additionally, to be accurate and conservative, a Table 7 of the FREL that 
presents the carbon density estimated for the amazon biome was used to get the carbon 
density in the project area.

1.5  Areas and spatial and temporary limits of the CCMP  
1.5.1 Total areas 
The Project is located in western region of the state of Mato Grosso along the border with 
Para comprising of the municipalities of Jacareacanga Para. The easier access to the project 
is via the city of Jacareacanga, Para.  
It is located within the territory constituted by the legally constituted indigenous reserve 
(See Map 1). The reserve is comprised primarily of dense Amazon Biome primary forest with 
a swath of land that is with natural non -forested area. From this area, the area of forests 
that have remained stable natural forests at the beginning of the reference period (2008 - 
2017) was analysed. This analysis yielded a forest eligible area for the project with a total of  
354 132.01 hectares.

Leakage potential area 
The leakage potential area is the discrete parcel(s) surrounding the project area in which, 
at the start of the CCMP, the deforestation in the project area may potential be displaced 
because of the CCMP.

The number of sampling plots was determined using Winrock’s CDM A/R sample 
plot calculator spreadsheet. This tool calculates the number of sample plots 
needed to estimate terrestrial carbon stocks, based on a specified targeted pre-
cision following the methodological tool “Calculation of the number of sample 
plots for measurements within A/R CDM project activities” and considering the 
conditions of each stratum present in the project. In this case, it is considered 
only one stratum (Ombrophile Dense Forest), the level of error selected was 5% 
and the confidence level 90%. The final plot quantity suggested by Winrock was 
22 plots of a size 625 m2 ha. However, 36 plots were installed. 
For each plot, data was collected from the arboreal stratum, collecting individu-
als with Diameter at the Chest Height (DCH) of more than 20 centimeters and 
for better ordering each plot was divided into subunits of 0.25 hectares. Each 
implemented plot rece ived an identification plate with the unit number, this

The implementation of the forest inventory in the REDD project area adopted 
the recommendations presented in the Cercarbono methodology, distributing 
the plots according to easy accessibility. The allometric equations used in the 
construction of the carbon map for the project are the same equations used in 
the Brazil’s submission of a Forest Reference Emission Level (FREL) for reducing 
emissions from deforestation in the Amazonia biome for REDD+  results-based 
payments under the UNFCCC from 2016 to 2020. Tho se equations are applied 
according with the diameter at breast height (DBH) of the sampled trees, as in-
dicated in the Equation below: 
 
For DBH ≥ 20 cm 
ln P = -0.151 + 2.170 × ln DBH 
Where: 
P = aboveground fresh biomass of a sampled tree; kg 
DBH = diameter at breast height of the sampled tree; cm 
 
For each sampled tree, the associated carbon density in the aboveground dry 
biomass was calculated from the aboveground fresh biomass of the tree apply-
ing the following Equation: 
C(CBH > 100 cm) = 0.2859 × P 
Where: 
P = aboveground fresh biomass of a sampled tree; kg 
C(CBH > 100 cm)  = carbon in the aboveground dry biomass of a tree with 
CBH>100cm; kg 
 
Because the RADAMBRASIL only sampled trees with circumference at breast 
height (CBH) above 100 cm (corresponding to diameter at breast height of 31.83 
cm), an extrapolation factor was applied to the average carbon stock of each 
sampled unit to include the carbon density of trees with CBH smaller than 100 
cm. This was based on the extrapolation of the histogram containing the range 
of CBH values observed in all sample units and the associated total number of 
trees (in intervals of 10 cm). 
• C(total) = 1.315698 × AC (CBH > 100 cm) 
Where: 
C(total) = total carbon stock of all trees in a sample unit; tC ha-1 
AC(CBH > 100 cm)  = total carbon stock in a sample unit from trees with CBH > 
100 cm; tC ha-1

7.1  Free and Prior Informed Conscent  
The project has conducted process of FPIC to continue the informative process initiated 
with the PRA to promote a reasonable understanding about what the project is and what 
their activities will do, it ensures an equitable participation in decision -making processes 
and the involvement of the population in the implementation of the proposed project, in 
this regard, we consider the following elements conductors for this process, avoiding the 
exercise of coercion, intimidation or manipulation (FREE);  
 
• Consent is required in advance to any authorization or beginning of the activities 
(PRIOR);  
• Providing information that covers the following information:  
• The nature, importance, rhythm, reversibility and approach of the project and the 
proposed activities.  
• The purpose of the project and its activities.  
• The duration of the project.  
• The area where the project and its activities were developed, as well as the localities 
involved.  
• The results of the initial diagnosis of the economic, social, cultural and environmen-
tal situation, including possible risks and benefits.  
• The institutions and staff that intervene in the implementation project; and  
• The procedures the project may include (claims resolution mechanism).  
• The consultation must be carried out through the establishment of a frank dialogue 
within an atmosphere of mutual respect, good faith and full and equitable partici-
pation (CONSENT);  
• The process must include genre perspective. Women participation is essential, as 
well as the involvement of children, young people and vulnerable groups.  
It is important to mention that the definite protocol for FPIC was produced and developed 
after experience from working on other REDD projects in the region.  This experience al-
lowed a duplication of the way that interviews were conducted with the local population.   
The following flowchart intends to represent the protocol to be followed in order to comply 
and ensure that the FPIC standards and criteria are implemented.

focused on temporary solutions to severe poverty, and many of the NGO’s basically gave 
out food. The first meeting with the chief consultation was held on June 1, 2011 with Celes-
tial Green Ventures.

8 Safeguards 
The UNFCCC defined in the 1CP/16 decision the measures to reduce emissions associated 
with deforestation, conservation, and enhancement of forest carbon stocks (REDD+). 
Within these measures, the Cancun Safeguards (the country where the conference took

Natural Risks 
The region in which the Project is located is not generally susceptible to severe or destruc-
tive natural events. However, the biggest fear is an expansion of the Cerrado land to the 
south, with a natural change from forest land to bushland, as the climate changes. With the 
reduction of illegal logging, this should not occur. However, the illegal loggers help this tran-
sition by altering the integrity of the native biome. 
The primary types of natural events that could occur would be geologic events, pests or 
disease, flooding, or a fire on the south side of the project area that could happen if it was 
man-made. The area is not prone to any geologic activity and poses little  to no risk to the 
Project. As the Project Area is a native and biodiversity ecosystem the risk from pests or 
diseases that result in significant emissions reversal is low. The primary mitigation for this 
risk is to maintain the forest and ensure through m onitoring that the trees and ecosystem 
remain healthy and intact. There can be minor seasonal flooding from the annual heavy rain 
season. However, the species of this area are all adapted to the hydrological cycles and are 
not liable to flooding. The Proje ct Area is not mountainous and there is not risk of erosion 
or landslides. 
The risk of human induced fire has the most potential to cause damage to the forests of the 
Project Area. However, the risk of significant emissions reversal is low. There have been no 
catastrophic fires in forests of this type in this region. Therefore, n atural events have low 
risks to the Project’s benefits.

14 Information management 
Based on the alignments of the measurement and quality control system recommended by 
the CMNUCC, the structure of the information quality management procedure related to 
greenhouse gas reductions is presented below, which comprises all actions, stakeholders, 
and support required to ensure quality during the implementation phase of the project. 
Data control and recording activities 
Quality control activities cover all the methods used to verify that the acquisition of data, 
the making of calculations, the estimation of air emissions, and the preparation of the doc-
ument are carried out correctly and reflect the reality of the project. This also includes ac-
tivity data, the technical reviews of emission sources, emission factors, and other parame-
ters used in the calculations. The results of the quality control activities allow  the adjust-
ment and correction of the emission estimates and u ncertainties, as well as identification 
of better opportunities. 
Communication channels 
The information from the field activities is based on clear and transparent evidence pro-
vided by the Munduruku people's association, community members and the technical team 
of environmental agents, which is subsequently shared with the consulting company Indig-
enous Carbon, which is supporting the project. 
In this way, in order to guarantee the documents that are requested to the Munduruku 
people, during the phases of the project, the consulting company Indigenous Carbon makes 
the electronic mail available. 
Firstly, in the preliminary phase and in the formulation phase of the project, the sending 
channel was the electronic mail of the project management, making a check list of docu-
mentation. As well as in the validation/verification/certification phase, the s ending will be 
by e-mail to the project management, due to the requirements sent by the certifier. In the 
project implementation phase, to deal with the commercialization and investments part, 
the sending will be by e-mail to the legal department. The othe r phases, such as receipt of 
requests, complaints, claims, or the like, will be sent by e -mail to the legal department, 
which will notify the receiver.

Management procedures 
It is considered fundamental to establish the following procedures for the management and 
control of documents: 
• Keep the information properly documented with their corresponding records, al-
ways seeking to facilitate the organization and search of documents, storing in fold-
ers according to each phase of the project. All documentation and information re-
lated to the project must be archived physically, when necessary, and digitally in 
Google Drive cloud during  the development of the project for at least 5 years. In 
addition, security copies of the information are made periodically to ensure conser-
vation and reproducibility. 
• Verify the pertinence of the documents before they are issued, ensuring the availa-
bility and validity of the resources. The professional responsible for receiving the 
documents delivers them to other members of the team, who verify the character-
istics, and only then the document and reports required are consolidated and pre-
pared. Once finalized, the final documents are made available by the project man-
agement in Google Drive the cloud. 
• Prioritize the management and availability of information related to all REDD+ activ-
ities, including calculations and projections, so that the information can be con-
sulted and validated by any citizen in different language and free of charge. In case 
there are levels of uncertainties and confidence intervals, the most conservative 
value is taken. In accordance with the principle of conservatism proposed by  ISO 
14064-2 and the CERCABONO protocol for voluntary carbon certification.

1.3  CCMP objective  
  
The project has a duration of 30 years and takes place in the Munduruku Indigenous Territory, 
in the municipality of Jacareacanga in Pará and has the objective of  strengthening the forces 
within the community to ensure environmental conservation and reduce GHG emissions from 
deforestation. It also promotes a decent living condition in the villages, generating benefits for 
all the population. 
The Munduruku people have a serious problem with illegal gold mining, thousands of hectares 
have been invaded by very dangerous illegal mining groups. The Government figures there are 
as many as 900 gold mines in the Munduruku Reserve, just outside of the carbon credit project 
area.  These mines are contaminating the forest, the rivers, the flora and the fauna with metals 
from the mining process.

1.4  CCMP description  
The Project is located in far southwest region of the state of Para.  The project has a total of 
354,132.01 hectares. After an analysis of agents and causes of deforestation, a leakage belt of 
a buffer project area of 2 km was defined. This leakage area includes 96,317.1 ha of forest 
area. The Project is structured as a 30 -year REDD project starting officially on July 1, 2017 
ending on June 30, 2047 that has the total participation of all of the community. The project 
foresees the reduction of emissions of 16,985,381 tCO2e during the 30 years of its useful life, 
that is, an average of 641,198 tCO2e per year. 
For this purpose, the implementation of a project Reduction of Emissions due to Deforestation 
is proposed. This will allow providing payments for emission reductions, considered an 
ecosystem service of the forests that the communities preserve through the care of the 
forests. 
Therefore, the collective territories linked to the project seek, through their territorial 
autonomy, to carry out conservation processes that preserve their cultural identity and 
promote the protection of the biodiversity and environmental wealth of their territory. 
Characteristics directly linked to the purpose of REDD+ projects, with the desired sustainable 
and sustainable local development, as well as to reduce emissions generated due to 
deforestation.

1.4.2.1.3 Leakage potential area 
The leakage potential area is the discrete parcel(s) surrounding the project area in which, at 
the start of the CCMP, the deforestation in the project area may potential be displaced 
because of the CCMP. 
For the determination of the leakage belt, a buffer width of 2 km was used, resulting in a 
leakage potential area of 201 632.00 ha for 2017. . However, according to the start date of the 
project, we only adopted the forest area within the leakage belt and the forest area within this 
belt is 96 317.12 ha on the project start date. 
The following criteria were used to determine the leakage potential area: 
a) The productive activities associated with the agents and causes of deforestation are the 
same as those that occur in the reference region and in the project area. 
b) The area of the leakage potential area is in the same biome as the project area. In 
addition, the biome between the project area and the leakage potential area is the 
same. 

--- Page 21 ---
 
 Rio Crepori REDD+ Project – Version 3.0

c) The adjacent micro -watersheds of the leakage potential area are from the same 
hydrographic zones as the project area. 
d) The stable forest area was determined in the same period as the reference period 
(2008 – 2017) 
e) The leakage potential area has forest areas close to the project area and meets the

1.6  Characteristics and conditions before the start of the CCMP  
1.6.1 Pre-Non-Isolated Status of the Community Group 
This indigenous people belong to the Munduruku linguistic family, of the Tupi branch, 
according to the knowledge disseminated orally among some elders, the designation 
Munduruku, as they have been known since the end of the 18th century, was the way they 
were called by the Parintintins, a rival people who were located in the region between the 
right bank of the Tapajós River and the Madeira River. This denomination would mean “red 
ants”, in allusion to the Munduruku warriors who attacked rival territories en masse. 

--- Page 33 ---
 
 Rio Crepori REDD+ Project – Version 3.0 
 
 
 
 33 
 
 
Also known as Mundurucu, Maytapu and Cara Preta, the Munduruku call themselves Wuy Jugu 
. The name Munduruku was given by rival groups and means red ants, an allusion to the fierce 
battle formations of the indigenous group. According to historical records, large contingents of 
warriors carried out surprise attacks at dawn, decimating rival adult populations, taking home 
the heads of their enemies as trophies. The heads were mummified, attributed to magical 
powers, placed on long spears and displayed in front of Munduruku villages. 
The sociolinguistic situation of the Munduruku is quite diverse, as a result of different 
moments in the history of contact with the colonization fronts, and because of the dispersion 
in different geographic spaces occupied by this people. The population located in the small 
villages on the banks of the Tapajós is mostly bilingual. In the Sai Cinza village, villages on the 
Cururu and Kabitutu rivers and other tributaries of the Tapajós, children, women and elderly 
people mostly speak only their mother tongue. There are also cases in which the Munduruku 
language goes through a process of disuse, with an almost exclusive domain of Portuguese, 
with children and young people who do not fully speak Munduruku, such as the villages of 
Mangue and Praia do Índio, located on the outskirts of the city of Itaituba, and in the 
communities of the Coatá-Laranjal Indigenous Land, in Amazonas. 
The Munduruku are located in different regions and territories in the states of Pará 
(southwest, channel and tributaries of the Tapajós river, in the municipalities of Santarém, 
Itaituba, Jacareacanga), Amazonas (east, Canumã river, municipality of Nova Olinda; and close 
to the Transamazônica, municipality of Borba), Mato Grosso (North, Rio dos Peixes region, 
municipality and Juara). They generally inhabit forested regions, on the banks of navigable 
rivers, and the traditional villages of the region of origin are located in the so -called “campos 
do Tapajós ”, classified among the occurrences of savannah in the interior of the Amazon 
forest. 
The Munduruku were only conquered by the colonists after several expeditions and rescue 
troops, organized by the Portuguese, were sent to the region, in retaliation for the resistance 
that the indigenous peoples presented through their attacks on the settlements. These attacks 
ended with the adoption of a supposedly friendly relationship that several scholars 
characterized as peace agreements between Munduruku chiefs and colonial authorities of the 
lower Tapajós interfluve, at the end of the 18th century, which led, for example, to the 
appeasement of relations with the residents. from the city of Santarém. 
As a result of the vast areas of their occupation and over which they transited, the 
Munduruku's contacts with the frontiers of expansion varied according to the proximity and 
ease of access to their territories. These factors resulted in the emergence of different aspects 
of the cultures of the Indians located on the banks of the Tapajós River, Madeira and Cururu 
rivers, and the lowland area known as Campos do Tapajós, a region where more traditional 
villages were located, and which is the scenario of good part of the mythology of this people.

1.6.2 Culture 
From the contact with economic fronts and non -indigenous institutions (mission and SPI), 
various aspects of the cultural life of the Munduruku underwent changes. As a warrior people, 
several significant cultural expressions were related to war activities, which had a striking 
symbolic character for the constitution of man and Munduruku society. The displacement of 
traditional villages to the establishment on the banks of the rivers, forming small population 
centers, certainly also contributed to the disappearance of the men's house, an important unit 
in the traditional village and the permanence of some rituals of a collective character that were 
related to the activities of provision of food, divided between the dry season (April to 
September) and the rainy season (October to March). Among these rituals was the “mother of 
the bush”, performed at the beginning of the rainy season, aiming to obtain permission for 
hunting activities, protection in incursions into the forest and good hunting results. Some 
elements of this activity are still present, or have been recreated with new meanings, 
especially in the respect relationship with the hunted animals, in the daily practices of the 
hunter to obtain game and in the dietary rules. 
The Munduruku maintain some cultural practices related to fishing, an activity of greater 
intensity in the summer, among which are the games that precede fishing with timbó, a root 
that after being crushed is used in rivers to facilitate the capture of fish. Usually the day before 
the “ tingejada ”, the timbó root is crushed on trunks, where it is rhythmically beaten with 
pieces of sticks by the men. Women, especially young women, gather annatto or the sap in the 
form of a white gum from a bush called rowan, and begin to pursue men with the aim of 
passing these products on their faces and hair; these flee and a game takes place throughout 
the village. For the Munduruku this is a way to make the fish happy and get plenty of fishing 
the next day. 
parasuy flutes, important instruments in Munduruku mythology, are still played periodically. 
But the players are old men, which compromises the continuity of the tradition. However, 
initiatives aimed at preserving traditional songs and music have emerged on the part of young 
people, especially teachers and new leaders. 
The wealth of Munduruku culture is extraordinary, including a repertoire of traditional songs 
of unusual musicality and poetry, which deals with everyday relationships, fruits, animals, etc. 
Cosmology presents narratives that include knowledge of the stars, constellations and the 
Milky Way, called kabikodepu, in which the stars that compose it are identified. 
Religiosity

In religious practices, shamans play a primordial role in healing through the manipulation of 
herbs, acts of smoking and contact with the world of spirits. Traditional religiosity is very 
present among the Munduruku, even with the changes suffered with colonization. Religiosity is 
present in all aspects of everyday life, governing relationships with nature, practices in the 
world of work and social relationships. 
There is the presence of two religious missions. The São Francisco Mission, located in the 
Missão village, on the Cururu river, installed in 1911; and the Batista Mission, which began its 
activities in the late 1960s, located in the Sai Cinza village, on the Tapajós River, about 40 
minutes by speedboat from the small town of Jacareacanga. As I said before, interferences in 
the cultural and religious life of the Munduruku are present due to the performance of the two 
religious institutions, however, the Munduruku for the most part, despite participating in 
Catholic and Protestant rituals, can hardly be considered as fully converted. Currently, there is 
no longer an open objection on the part of the Missions to pajelança practices. And it seems 
that the Munduruku do not attach great importance to the condemnations made by the 
Christian religions of their traditional religiosity. The presence of missions of different religions 
did not cause rivalries or disputes of this nature among the Munduruku, a fact that may mean 
that they attribute their own solutions and interpretations with regard to religion. 
Material culture 
In material culture, basketry and braiding stand out, which are masculine activities, with men 
making the Iço – a basket with which women carry the fruits and products of the countryside –
, the sieves and other household utensils made with splints. and natural fibers. 
In Munduruku baskets, drawings that identify the husband's clan are engraved with urucu. 
Thus, for example, the slings for carrying children, made by women from fiber extracted from a 
tree, identify, with the natural red or white color, the exogamous moiety to which the child 
belongs. 
Some men and especially women are expert in making necklaces with zoomorphic figures (fish, 
tracajás, wildcat, alligator, etc.) sculpted with inajá and tucumã seeds. 
Pottery, a feminine activity par excellence, is almost disappeared, with some women in the 
Kaburuá and Katõ villages who still master traditional techniques. There is information that 
among the Munduruku of the Coatá indigenous land, in the state of Amazonas, this practice is 
more present. 
The weaving, mainly of cotton nets, is also in disuse, despite having a considerable number of 
adult and elderly women who have knowledge of the technique and sometimes make for sale 
as handicrafts. 
Productive system

The livelihoods related to the production and procurement of food among the Munduruku are 
preponderantly in the field of traditional economy, despite the inclusion of some non -
indigenous products in their eating habits, which need to be purchased regularly, of which salt 
is the most common, coffee and sugar. 
Agriculture is practiced according to immemorial knowledge, on dry land, with full use of 
spaces and the intercropping of crops. The most common crops are the different types of 
cassava, bananas, potatoes, sugarcane and yams. Fruit trees are most often planted on paths 
to gardens. 
In the social division of labor, it is up to the man to drill and cut down the forest where the 
stump swidden will be opened. The coivara, cleaning after the fire, is normally done by the 
whole family. The planting of cassava is done with the participation of men and women; other 
crops such as potatoes, yams, pineapples and peppers are carried out only by women. 
Normally, the activities of weeding the gardens and harvesting are carried out by women. 
Activities such as fishing, hunting and gathering have relevance in obtaining food and are 
organized according to the seasons. Fishing is certainly currently the main way to obtain 
animal protein, being carried out daily in the dry season with good results, and less practiced in 
the rainy season, when the rivers flood, forming igapós and making the activity difficult. 
Fruit collection is carried out at different times of the year according to the harvest of each 
fruit tree (açaí, patauá, bacaba, uxi, jubá , pupunha, murici, ingá, chestnut, etc.). The dense 
juices, called wines in the region, play an important role in food, especially in the rainy season, 
when fish becomes scarce, and make up, alongside flour and game meat, the basis of food in 
winter. 
As for the means of obtaining income that make it possible to purchase products (salt, sugar, 
soap, clothes, sandals, fuel, etc.), the Munduruku currently carry out flour production activities 
in some communities on the Tapajós River, and the collection of nuts in many communities.

due to the low prices offered. As discussed in the item “Contact History”, the Munduruku 
served as labor in the heyday of rubber extraction, so this activity ended up being incorporated

After the fall in rubber prices, the Tapajós region was discovered in the late 1950s as a major 
gold producer. This movement intensified after the construction of the Transamazônica 
highway, in 1972, and had its peak in the period from 1975 to 90. (working with pans in places 
already explored by mining machines, in an attempt to find gold sparks) during the period of 
intense exploration of the barge mines on the Tapajós and São Manoel rivers, or visiting the 
explorations of non -Indians in the lowland mines (name given to the mining work place, 
formed by rectangular excavations on the banks of rivers made with the use of tools and

Indigenous organizations 
The Munduruku participated in the second Assembly of Indigenous Chiefs held in Brazil, which 
took place in May 1975, in the village Missão Cururu, with the presence of leaders of various 
ethnicities (the first Assembly took place at the headquarters of Missão Anchieta, in April 1974, 
and did not have Munduruku representatives). The first Assemblies on the initiative of the 
leaders and with the participation of chiefs and representatives of most Munduruku villages 
took place in 1985/86, and had as main theme the issue of land demarcation, in addition to 
discussing problems related to education, health, environment and projects aimed at the 
economy of communities. But the meetings only started to be registered after the 1st General 
Assembly of the Munduruku People was held, in 1989. Over the years, the organization 
matured, participation grew and discussions expanded. 
Pusuru Indigenous Association in 1991, on the initiative of some leaders and with the aim of 
organizing claims for the demarcation of the land, as well as developing actions related to the 
defense of the environment. , education, health and other problems faced by the population. 
In the same year, the leaders understood that a form of organization was needed that 
exercised a more direct political role, guiding the discussions and allowing the broad 
participation of representatives from various Munduruku communities. Then came the 
Munduruku Indigenous Council of Alto Tapajós (CIMAT). 
In 2002, the XIV General Assembly was held, the first after the conclusion of the land 
demarcation work, for which many leaders together with their communities fought. 
However, the challenges are many. The difficult location, among other factors, discourages 
more constant exchange relationships with other indigenous entities, knowledge of other 
experiences and the search for allies to face contemporary problems. The organization of the 
Munduruku, like that of many indigenous peoples in Brazil, lives in a situation of near isolation

School 
Another aspect worth mentioning in the Munduruku organization process is the interest they 
have always had in improving school education. Many of the existing schools emerged at the 
initiative of the communities, and several indigenous teachers worked for years as volunteers, 
contributing to literacy and the feeling of commitment of many young people who are today 
participating in actions of community interest. The training work for the first teachers began in 
the mid-1970s, with support from SIL (Sociedade Internacional de Linguística) and Missão São 
Francisco. 
After a long break, school activities resumed with a new format and new principles in the late 
1980s, some at the initiative of CIMI (Indigenist Missionary Council) and others by Funai. The 
Munduruku Indigenous Teacher Training Project is currently in effect, under the coordination 
of Funai and in partnership with the Indigenous Education Section of SEDUC -PA (Secretariat of 
Education of Pará), also counting on the support of the Munduruku and of the Baptist Mission 
and Cururu Mission. The course, which is modular and started in 1998, is in the process of 
being recognized by the State Council of Education of Pará.

1.6.5.2. Hidrography 
The Tapajós River is a river that rises in the state of Mato Grosso, bathes part of the state of 
Pará and flows into the Amazon River, still in the state of Pará, in front of the city of Santarém, 
about 695 kilometers from Belém. 
The name Tapajós originates from an indigenous tribe on the banks of the river. The Tapajós 
originates at the confluence of the Juruena and São Manuel rivers (Teles Pires). 
When combined with the Juruena River, the Tapajós is approximately 1900 km long. 
Most of its route is in the state of Pará, but the upper part (south) borders the states of Pará 
and Amazonas. The Tapajós River basin covers 6% of the waters of the Amazon basin, being 
the fifth largest basin in the system. 
Due to its great extension, the Tapajós River, unfortunately, is constantly a place where many 
people disappear and often die.

1.6.5.3. Geology and Geomorphology 
The geology of Jacareacanga area in the southwestern and south eastern parts of the states of 
Amazonas and Pará, is presented here in terms of its main lithostratigraphic units, structural 
framework and mineral resources (gold) characteristics, as well as its geological evolution.  

--- Page 55 ---
 
 Rio Crepori REDD+ Project – Version 3.0 
 
 
 
 55 
 
 
The Paleoproterozoic age is represented by the Cuiú -Cuiú Complex, Jacareacanga Group, 
Parauari Intrusive Suite, Iriri Group, Maloquinha Intrusive Suite and Buiuçu formation. The 
Cuiú-Cuiú  
Complex consists of orthogneiss and granitoid plutons (tonalitic to granodioritic in 
composition), and minor amphibolite, diorite and rarely garnet bearing leucogranite. Several 
authors consider the Jacareacanga Group a greenstone belt sequence.  
It includes two main domains: quartzitic domain (quartzite, metachert and banded iron 
formation units) and a schistose do main (mica schist, quartz schist and rare actinolite -
tremolite schist and talc schist).  
Both of them are intruded generally by granitoid bodies of the Parauari Intrusive Suite (sub -
divided in granitic and granodioritic facies), the Maloquinha Intrusive Suite (alaskitic granite 
subdivided in amphibole -bearing and biotite -bearing facies), the Pepita Granite (riebeckite -
arfvedsonite alkali feldspar granite) and also by Caroçal Granite (monzogranite to sienogranite 
and volcanic rocks of the Iriri Group (rhyolite, dacite and locally tuff and ignimbrite).  
The Jacareacanga Group is unconformably overlain by the Buiuçu Formation (arkose 
sandstone, conglomeratic sandstone with minor interbedded tuff units). Paleozoic 
Sedimentary rocks are represented by the Jatuarana Group (Siluro -Devonian) and the Ipixuna 
Formation (Permo-Carboniferous). Jatuarana Group is formed, in decreasing order of age, by 
the Borrachudo, Capoeiras and São Benedito formations. The Jurassic Periquito Dolerite 
generally crosscuts this Paleozoic cover.  
Two main structural features are observed: 1) regional foliation with NNE -SSW and NNW -SSE 
trends (only basement rocks) and 2) main oblique strike -slip shear zones with NW-SE trend (on 
Parauari granitic bodies and basement rocks, mainly). The Tapajós region was initially affected 
by crust generation in the Archean-Paleoproterozoic boundary (2,5 Ga).  
However, the major units are formed during the Paleoproterozoic (2,0 to 1,9 Ga) with the 
production of large volumes of arc -related magma, generating juvenile continental crust in a 
collisional setting. 
 Several post-collisional granite intrusions (of ten A -type), mafic dyke swarms and sedimentary 
basins were developed in extensional settings.  
A wide variety of gold mineralization styles occur in the Jacareacanga region including that 
shear zone-quartz vein, quartz lode and porphyry-hosted stockwork/disseminated types.  
In total 37 small -scale pros pec tor´s workings (garimpos) were identified in the area. Two 
hundred and four occurrences were described, including those for pyrite, cassiterite, 
turmaline, thorite, zircon, topaz, xenotime, monazite, fluorite and also potential areas for 
industrial minerals.

The Jacareacanga Revolt was a rebellion by the Air Force, led by Major Haroldo Veloso and 
Captain José Chaves Lameirão, who took over the military base of Jacareacanga, in Pará.  
It consisted of a reaction against the inauguration of Juscelino Kubitschek, and his government 
was seen by the leaders of the revolt as the return of the government inspired by Getúlio 
Vargas.  
It has connections with the November 11 coup movement, which took place in the previous 
year, 1955. It began on the night of February 10, 1956, when the two officers took an AT -11 
fighter plane in Rio de Janeiro.  
During the 19 days of revolt, the city of Santarém and some other small villages were taken 
over by the rebels, and the government found it difficult to reprimand the movement, even 
more so because of the refusal of the Air Force to help in this process.  
On the 29th of the same month and year, the revolt ended, after being controlled by loyalist 
troops, with the arrest of one of its leaders, Haroldo Veloso.

carried out within TI Kayabi. The Munduruku community did not allow the team access to their

Kayabi Indigenous Land 
The Kayabi IT is located in the municipalities of Jacareacanga, PA, and Apiacás, MT, and has 
eight villages: Kururuzinho, Tukumã, Minhocoçu, Coelho, São Benedito, Mairowi, Sapezal and 
Teles Pires. The Kuruzinho village has the best infrastructure. 
It has a health center, telephone, radio, running water, an electricity generator that works four 
hours a day and a school that serves all students in the region. 
In the Kayabi IT live Indians from the Kayabi, Apiaká and Munduruku *ethnicities. In 2007, 
approximately 900 people lived in this Indigenous Land, 190 from the Kayabi ethnic group, 160 
from the Apiaká ethnic group and 550 from the Munduruku ethnicity. 
As with most indigenous groups in Brazil, hunting and fishing are very important activities for 
the Indians who live there, who also have an agricultural tradition and appreciate and grow 
fruit. They produce handicrafts, such as basketry and woodwork, typically male activities, and 
ceramics and weaving, practiced by women. 
The Teles Pires River is important to the Kayabi community for fishing, navigation and also as 
part of their beliefs and rituals. An example of a traditional practice in the Kururuzinho village 
is the *rite of male initiation.

Flora 
The main vegetation type in Jacareacanga is the Amazon Rainforest, which is very rich in 
species. Studies have identified more than 850 plant species. 
There are two types of forest in the area, terra firme forest and alluvial forest. The terra firme 
forest is located in the higher parts of the land, where the river does not reach. It is a lush 
forest, with tall trees with a closed canopy. A typical tree in this forest is the chestnut tree. 
Alluvial forest occurs in the lower parts, which are flooded during floods, on the banks and on 
the islands. There are also tall trees, which stand out from the others, such as the cariperana 
and the jacareúba, and the buriti and açaí palms can still be found. 
Among the trees found in the region, the chestnut, the angelim -pedra and the maçaranduba 
stand out, the latter two of great commercial value and which are threatened with extinction.

 Analysis of the Legal Framework 
In Brazil, the current legislation does not contemplate a regularization for the carbon market, 
thus the commercialization of carbon credits occurs in the voluntary forest carbon market, 
recognized by the National Commission for REDD+ in Resolution N03 of 2020 . The legislation 
related to REDD+ projects can be checked on the Ministry of Environment's website, in the 
Brazil REDD+ section: Related Legislation (mma.gov.br) 
Furthermore, as it is an indigenous land that was homologated and registered in 2004, 
according to the search website of the Instituto SocioAmbiental , the Munduruku people have

permanent possession of the territory they inhabit and the right to the exclusive usufruct of 
the natural riches and all the utilities on those lands, in accordance with the Brazilian 
Constitution of 1988 and the Indian Statute of 1973. 
It is a type of project that is not only the result of compliance with a regulation defined in the 
context of climate change , n or is it only an environmental offset.  However, the project is a 
voluntary initiative by the Munduruku people to protect their indigenous territory and the 
forest as a strategy to secure a financial opportunity that generates benefits for everyone in 
the community and offers new paths of sustainable socio -environmental development for the 
villages. The reserve is a land owned by the indigenous people, which has no other initiatives 
or certification programs, and there are no other initiatives that are funding REDD+ activities.

Barrier analysis: 
• Investment/financing: 
Establishing improvements in the quality of life in the villages, better income opportunities for 
indigenous people, and greater control and oversight of the reserve can occur with resources 
provided by the state or by national or international investment. However, the advancement 
of activities aimed at strengthening the governance of the indigenous territory, improving local 
infrastructure, and monitoring the perimeter do not generate profitability, and 
implementation depends on financial aid.  
• Technological: 
The indigenous population of Munduruku lacks adequate education and structure in schools. 
As there is no technical training for the indigenous people to be professionalized and develop 
profitable activities in the villages. In addition, they need updated training to monitor the 
territory using new technologies and new techniques to prevent invasions, fires, and 
contamination.

2.5.1 Analysis of actors and drivers of deforestation  
The causes of deforestation originating from anthropic activities are those human actions that 
are carried out at the local level on a forest, such as the expansion of the frontier of agriculture 
and/or livestock, the implementation of infrastructure projects, forced displacement, illegal 
mining or the selective use of forest species, either to obtain wood or other uses that involve 
the felling of individuals, directly impacting the natural vegetation cover. Although there are 
also causes of natural origin that are delimited by the biophysical conditions of the territories.  
Those of anthropic origin are subject to local and regional contexts due to underlying causes 
that can be demographic, economic, technological, cultural and institutional, which are 
particular to each of the territories and are not always so clear to elucidate.  
In such a way that, to identify the agents and drivers of deforestation in the project area, it is 
necessary to describe the context in which these agents and drivers converge, and for which 
information sources were consulted. that have a direct relationship with the territory, either 
from the point of land tenure, as is the case of the diagnoses carried out, from the perspective 
of managing and regulating the use of natural resources, as is the case with the environmental 
authority; from the figure of management and coordination as is the case of regional leaders 
such as the mayors of the municipality or the governors of the states.

2.5.2.2 Interpretation and classification 
The method of classification of satellite images used by PRODES follows four main steps. First a 
spectral mixing model is generated identifying the components of vegetation, soil and shade. 
This technique is known as a linear spectral mixture model (MLME) that aims to estimate the 
percentage of vegetation, soil and shade components for each cell (pixel) of the satellite 
image. The second step is the application of the segmentation technique, which identifies in 
the satellite image spatially adjacent regions (segments) with similar spectral characteristics. 
After segmentation, the segments are categorized individually to identify the forest, non-forest 
vegetation, hydrography and deforestation classes (anthropic vegetation). Finally, the result of 
classified segmentation is submitted to the process of editing or auditing the classification, 
performed by a specialist and ending with the creation of state mosaics.

2.5.3  Conversion of forest land into gold mining land 
Gold mining can cause deforestation, water pollution and soil contamination. Deforestation 
occurs when the forest is cleared to make room for mines. Water pollution occurs when 
mercury, a heavy metal, is used to separate gold from rock. Mercury can contaminate rivers 
and lakes, affecting fish and other aquatic animals. Soil contamination occurs when mercury 
and other mining waste is dumped into the soil.  
Gold mining can also have negative social impacts. Miners often work in dangerous and 
unhealthy conditions. They can also be exposed to mercury and other toxic chemicals. Gold 
mining can also lead to conflicts between miners and indigenous communities.  
Gold mining can generate jobs and income for local communities. However, the economic 
benefits of gold mining are often concentrated in the hands of a small number of companies 
and individuals. 
Gold mining is one of the main drivers of deforestation in the Amazon. According to the 
National Institute for Space Research (Inpe), gold mining was responsible for 15% of 
deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon between 2015 and 2020. 
Gold mining also contributes to greenhouse gas emissions. Deforestation caused by gold 
mining releases carbon from the forest into the atmosphere. Mercury used in gold mining can 
also contribute to greenhouse gas emissions, as it can be released into the atmosphere when 
burned.

Based on the type of agriculture advanced by the indigenous communities, it is highlighted 
that the method of cultivation through the mandioca of cutting down one and a half hectares, 
approximately for each product, preceded by burning, planting and harvesting in has an 
insignificant effect on the overall forest and is constitutionally protected right of the 
indigenous, given that the indigenous are experts in their culture, they rarely have a fire 
become out of control. 
The type of agriculture, advanced by the communities, is low -scale non-commercial crops. This 
driver is also due to the limited technical capacity to establish sustainable establishment and

sustainable. These sustenance plots do not greatly expand further into the forest because of

This deforestation engine is creating a negligible amount of carbon emissions.

2.5.7  Unsustainable extraction of timber and non-timber forest products 
According to information from a report completed by the FUNAI office in Cocoal, Rodonia, the 
FUNAI office is responsible for the reserve. The primary deforestation of the reserve is from

Also, it can be seen in the area some small areas with indirect processes of deforestation due

biomass content. These areas are generally found on the edges of the various roads that pass

Regarding non -timber forest products (NTFPs), it is recognized that NTFPs are important for 
the well -being of many rural communities and contribute to the conservation processes of 
tropical forests. 
Even the though the use of forest products is an activity that has been developed for 
thousands of years, only in the last forty years have NTFPs become an object of interest 
worldwide, due, among other reasons, to the concern that occurred at the end of the eighties 
around environmental problems, deforestation and the well -being of communities (FAO, 
1991). 
They have been used to investigate options to face poverty and conserve the environment, 
through diversification strategies of the different productive activities, seeking improvements 
in the income of local communities, provision of food security and protection of biological and 
cultural diversity. (De la Peña & Illsley, 2001). 
However, the current prospects for the use of NTFPs cause their overuse or overexploitation, 
leading to an affectation of the native populations with strong ecological and economic 
implications, due to the lack of criteria for their sustainable use and the control of the actors 
involved in its marketing.

The number of sampling plots was determined using Winrock’s CDM A/R sample plot 
calculator spreadsheet. This tool calculates the number of sample plots needed to estimate 
terrestrial carbon stocks, based on a specified targeted precision following the methodological 
tool “Calculation of the number of sample plots for measurements within A/R CDM project 
activities” and considering the conditions of each stratum present in the project. In this case, it 
is considered only one stratum (Ombrophile Dense Forest), the level of error selected was 5% 
and the confidence level 90%. The final plot quantity suggested by Winrock was 22 plots of a 
size 625 m2 ha. However, 36 plots were installed. 
For each plot, data was collected from the arboreal stratum, collecting individuals with 
Diameter at the Chest Height (DCH) of more than 20 centimeters and for better ordering each

project are the same equations used in the Brazil’s submission of a Forest Reference Emission 
Level (FREL) for reducing emissions from deforestation in the Amazonia biome for REDD+ 
results-based payments under the UNFCCC from 2016 to 2020. Those equations are applied

Where: 
P = aboveground fresh biomass of a sampled tree; kg 
DBH = diameter at breast height of the sampled tree; cm 
For each sampled tree, the associated carbon density in the aboveground dry bi omass was

C(CBH > 100 cm) = 0.2859 × P

P = aboveground fresh biomass of a sampled tree; kg

factor was applied to the average carbon stock of each sampled unit to include the carbon 
density of trees with CBH smaller than 100 cm. This was based on the extrapolation of the 
histogram containing the range of CBH values observed in all sample units and the associated 
total number of trees (in intervals of 10 cm). 
C(total) = 1.315698 × AC (CBH > 100 cm)

3.2  Quantification of GHG emissions and removals or GHG emission 
reductions in project scenario  
The project's GHG emission reductions were calculated based on the annual loss of forest 
cover from the baseline, in hectares of deforestation avoided by the project's action. It is 
assumed in that the effectiveness of the project to avoid deforestation will be 95% 
(Effectiveness Index, EI) . This value is considered the maximum possible effectiveness of the 
project to avoid deforestation and that is why it is maintained in the following years during the 
life of the project. The percentages of effectiveness will be subject to modifications in the 
subsequent revisions of the baseline.  
Therefore, the areas to be deforested in in the project area was determined by multiplying the 
deforestation rate determined by the following equation:

3.3  Leakage  
An estimation of potential leakage emissions resulting from the CCMP (for the deforestation 
segment) was made based on percentage increases in deforestation over the estimated annual 
deforestation projection for the project area and applying the same factors and calculation 
methods used for the project area.  
The source of leakage monitored were:  
● Displacement by grazing and livestock production 
● leakage due to displacement activity.  
● Displacement due to agricultural activities 
● Increased use of fertilisers 
● Wood harvesting 
● Deforestation 
Leakage due to displacement activity was monitored by mapping forest cover change in the 
leakage potential area. Activity data for the leakage belt area was determined using the same 
methods applied to deforestation mapping in the Project area. The following table present the 
annual areas of deforestation in the leakage area in the project scenario. 
Considering the monitoring and control of deforestation, the strengthening of institutional 
governance, the project assumes  15% as “leakage displacement factor” because not all 
deforestation agents do not participate in leakage prevention and project activities.  Therefore 
421.26 ha could be deforested in the leakage belt during the project length.

4.2  LINK with NDCs  
 
The Paris Agreement signed in 2015 had as its main goal not to allow the planet to warm more 
than 1.5°C by the end of the 21st century.  Thus, each country est ablished its targets for 
reducing greenhouse gas emissions, called Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC).  
Brazil, according to 2019 data from the NGO World Resources Institute, is the seventh largest 
emitter of greenhouse gases, accounting for about 3% of global emissions and representing a 
significant role in climate change. 
So, in a first moment, the country defined its commitment with the Paris Agreement to reduce 
37% by 2025 and 43% by 2030, in relation to 2005. In 2021 it committed to increase the goal to 
50% by 2030 and to reach neutral emissions by 2050, that is, everything the country emits 
must be offset with carbon capture sources. 
Considering that approximately half of Brazilian emissions are due to deforestation and forest 
fires, REDD+ projects work as a crucial strategy to help the country, even though it's a 
volunteer project. Because the projects promote the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions in 
Brazil through avoided deforestation, that is, forest conservation prevents millions of tons of 
CO2 from being released into the atmosphere. So even though this is a voluntary carbon 
market project, it is aligned with the UN Agenda and has a positive impact on Brazil’s.

The decision-making process is based on meetings between the leadership of all the villages. 
The villagers elect their leader, and this leader represents the voice of the residents in the 
village. The leadership have regular meetings to discuss many subjects – and the carbon credit 
project has been a topic added to those meetings since the project started. Culturally, the 
Munduruku people solve their problems and questions verbally, right away, and define the 
responsibilities for the next steps. It is not very common to fill up meetings minutes or 
attendance sheets. 
The grievance redressal policy also follows their culture, in which the matters are solved 
verbally. It was defined that the complaints and questions from the outsiders of the villages 
will be written down in detail, but the internal doubts, questions or request will be managed as 
their culture defined ever since, and they don’t have the need to be noted. For the Munduruku 
people, a word is still valid and appreciated, in some cases, even more than words written in 
papers.

Natural Risks 
The region in which the Project is located is not generally susceptible to severe or destructive 
natural events. However, the biggest fear is an expansion of the Cerrado land to the south, 
with a natural change from forest land to bushland, as the climate changes. With the reduction 
of illegal logging, this should not occur. However, the illegal loggers help this transition by 
altering the integrity of the native biome. 
The primary types of natural events that could occur would be geologic events, pests or 
disease, flooding, or a fire on the south side of the project area that could happen if it was 
man-made. The area is not prone to any geologic activity and poses little to no risk to the 
Project. As the Project Area is a native and biodiversity ecosystem the risk from pests or 
diseases that result in significant emissions reversal is low. The primary mitigation for this risk 
is to maintain the forest and ensure through monitoring that the trees and ecosystem remain 
healthy and intact. There can be minor seasonal flooding from the annual heavy rain season. 
However, the species of this area are all adapted to the hydrological cycles and are not liable 
to flooding. The Project Area is not mountainous and there is  not risk of erosion or landslides. 
The risk of human induced fire has the most potential to cause damage to the forests of the 
Project Area. However, the risk of significant emissions reversal is low. There have been no 
catastrophic fires in forests of this type in this region. Therefore, natural events have low risks 
to the Project’s benefits.

The Project has reduced the risk of leakage, illegal logging, and fire by building strong 
partnerships with the households in the Project Boundaries and its vicinity thus preventing 
deforestation activities to start. Also, capacity -building workshops were held to better monitor 
the forest, thus preventing further land use change in the area.

Community activities are designed to transform local economies over the life of the Project. In 
this regard, the focus of Munduruku developed local business and income-generating activities 
that are critical components of a long -term low carbon economy. Project activities that met 
this overarching objective focus on education, sustainable agriculture, community -based 
ecotourism, and sustainable management of natural resources. These activities reduced the 
necessity of community members to deforest and degrade the Project Area. During the Project 
Lifetime, this is achieved, for example, by facilitating better education, through training 
farmers in sustainable agriculture.

Monitoring Deforestation and Project Emissions 
Forest cover change due to unplanned deforestation is monitored through periodic 
assessment of classified satellite imagery covering the project area. Emissions from 
deforestation are estimated by multiplying the detected area of forest loss by the average 
forest carbon stock per unit area. 
The project boundary, as set out in the PD, will serve as the initial “forest cover benchmark 
map” against which changes in forest cover will be assessed over the interval of the monitoring 

--- Page 185 ---

period. The entire project area has been demonstrated to meet the forest definition at the 
beginning of the crediting period. For subsequent monitoring periods, change in forest cover 
will be assessed against the preceding classified forest cover map marking the beginning of the 
monitoring interval. The resulting classified image is compared with the preceding classified 
image (forest cover benchmark map marking the start of the monitoring interval) to detect 
forest cover change over the monitoring interval, and subsequently becomes the updated 
forest cover benchmark map for the next monitoring interval. Thus, the forest benchmark map 
is updated at each monitoring event. 
The increase or decrease in carbon stocks due to planned activities in the project area will also 
be monitored through documents and periodic assessment of classified satellite imagery 
covering the project area. In case of planned deforestation, emissions are estimated by 
multiplying the area of forest loss by the average forest carbon stock per unit area. 
As this monitoring will be conducted mainly by using remote sensing imagery in a GIS 
environment, quality management procedures are related to GIS data quality. When working 
with geographical information, positional accuracy is often synonymous with data quality. Data 
compilation from several different sources often requires very good data quality. Quality 
procedures must be employed to ensure that data are properly collected, handled, processed, 
used and maintained throughout the data lifecycle while performing monitoring activities.

Positional accuracy in satellite images 
It is very important to ensure that remote sensing images in a time series overlay properly with 
each other and with other GIS maps used in the analysis. To geometrically correct the acquired 
images, it is necessary to have at least one orthorectified image to use as a reference image 
and to undertake a process called geo-referencing. 
Images were geometrically corrected to the projection UTM Zone 22 South datum WGS 1984 
using an orthorectified image by collecting manually selected control points in both images. 
Among the features to be identified as control point locations we have road or stream 
intersections, the mouth of a stream, the corner of an established plot, or road corners. The 
second-order polynomial transformation and the nearest neighbor resampling technique could

correction process were acceptable.

The calculation procedure for estimating leakage emissions in the project scenario will be done 
by monitoring the following sources of leakage: 
- Carbon stock changes and GHG emissions associated with leakage prevention activities. 
The carbon stock decrease due to leakage prevention measures, which will probably take place 
inside the leakage management area, will be monitored through documents and field 
assessment. 
In areas undergoing carbon stock enhancement, the project conservatively assumes stable 
stocks and no biomass monitoring is conducted. 
- Carbon stock decrease and increases in GHG emissions due to activity displacement leakage. 
Deforestation in the leakage potential area may be considered activity displacement leakage. 
Activity data for the leakage potential area will be determined using the same methods applied 
to monitoring deforestation activity data in the project area. Furthermore, GHG emissions 
from displaced forest fires within the leakage potential area will also be accounted, if 
significant. 
Leakage will be calculated by comparing the ex ante and the ex post assessment. However, 
where strong evidence can be collected that deforestation in the leakage belt is attributable to 
deforestation agents that are not linked to the project area, the detected deforestation will 
not be attributed to the project activity, thus not considered leakage. 
Monitoring of Natural Disturbance and catastrophic events  
The carbon stock losses within the project area will be estimated as soon as possible after the 
natural event, e.g. uncontrolled forest fires and other catastrophic events.

people, during the phases of the project, the consulting company Indigenous Carbon makes 
the electronic mail available. 
Firstly, in the preliminary phase and in the formulation phase of the project, the sending 
channel was the electronic mail of the project management, making a check list of 
documentation. As well as in the validation/verification/certification phase, the sending will be 
by e -mail to the project management, due to the requirements sent by the certifier. In the 
project implementation phase, to deal with the commercialization and investments part, the 
sending will be by e -mail to the legal department. The other phases, such as receipt of 
requests, complaints, claims, or the like, will be sent by e -mail to the legal department, which 
will notify the receiver. 
Management procedures 
It is considered fundamental to establish the following procedures for the management and 
control of documents: 
• Keep the information properly documented with their corresponding records, always 
seeking to facilitate the organization and search of documents, storing in folders 
according to each phase of the project. All documentation and information related to 
the project must be archived physically, when necessary, and digitally in Google Drive 
cloud during the development of the project for at least 5 years. In addition, security 
copies of the information are made periodically to ensure conservation and 
reproducibility. 
• Verify the pertinence of the documents before they are issued, ensuring the availability 
and validity of the resources. The professional responsible for receiving the documents 
delivers them to other members of the team, who verify the characteristics, and only 
then the document and reports required are consolidated and prepared. Once 
finalized, the final documents are made available by the project management in Google 
Drive the cloud. 
• Prioritize the management and availability of information related to all REDD+ 
activities, including calculations and projections, so that the information can be 
consulted and validated by any citizen in different language and free of charge. In case 
there are levels of uncertainties and confidence intervals, the most conservative value 
is taken. In accordance with the principle of conservatism proposed by the CERCABONO 
protocol for voluntary carbon certification.
