1.3  CCMP Objective  
The main objective of the Pampa-1 CCMP is to generate carbon credits for GHG emis-
sions removals under Cercarbono’s Voluntary Carbon Certification Program for a 30-
year period. This objective will be achieved through afforestation with eucalypt of 
grazing and agricultural lands in the Buenos Aires province, Argentina. Once the trees 
are fully established, the cattle will be allowed back to the project area, where they 
will have better living conditions due to the shade. 
1.4  CCMP Description  
The Silvopastoral Afforestation in Pampa-1 CCMP (hereafter CCMP) is located in the 
Pampean Plain, central-west region of Argentina. It is the most intensively modified 
region of the country, as it is now covered by artificial grasslands and agricultural 
lands with almost no tree cover and few fragments of the native ecosystem (Pereyra, 
2012). The project takes place in a small portion of the Fortín Paunero Establishment, 
a private property dedicated to raising cattle since 1899.  
The CCMP consists of one reforestation segment composed by the afforesta-
tion of seven neighboring lots that add up 95,41 eligible hectares with Eucalyptus 
spp. to provide shade for cattle. 95,12 ha were planted with E. viminalis, and 0,29 ha 
were planted with E. camaldulensis and E. grandis. At the start of the project’s activi-
ties, cattle will be excluded from the project area to allow the trees to grow and de-
velop properly. After 6 years, thinning will be carried out and the cattle will be allowed 
back in. The new conditions in the project area will diminish heat stress and increase 
the cattle’s welfare whilst increasing productivity  (Bottegal, n.d.). The project has a 
lifetime of 30 years (starting on 2024.09.21 and ending on 2054.09.21), with an initial 
20-year accreditation period (from 2024.09.21 to 2044.09.21). 
 The initial state of the project area has no trees, and under the baseline sce-
nario the property would remain without any forest cover. Hence, the main carbon 
pools in the project scenario are above and belowground tree biomass, with an esti-
mated average annual removal of 2.490 t CO2e and a total removal of 74.706 t CO2e 
throughout the project’s lifetime. According to the methodology, since the only emis-
sion sources in the project scenario come from the planting activity, they are not con-
sidered. Additionally, the cattle that is excluded from the project area will not be dis-
placed outside of the Fortín Paunero property, so no leakage will be generated in this 
regard. 
 The project was designed under Cercarbono’s M/LU/F -A01 v1.1 methodology 
(hereafter methodology) and complies with Cercarbono’s Protocol for Voluntary Car-
bon Certification v 4. 4 (hereafter protocol). This document provides the necessary 
information to ensure that the CCMP complies with all Cercarbono’s requirements and 
principles as stated in aforementioned methodology and program to validate and ver-
ify the emissions removals. The carbon credits generated by this CCMP will be sold in 
the voluntary carbon market. 
GHG type Activity that generates or reduces it 
CO2 Emission reductions from afforestation of grazing lands with 
Eucalyptus viminalis,E. camaldulensis and E. grandis.

1.4.1 Sectoral Scope and Type of CCMP 
According to the protocol, this CCMP belongs to the Land Use sector as it will take 
place in a grass land and agricultural area. Additionally, it classifies as a Type 2 be-
cause it will remove less than 10,000 t CO 2e per year through afforestation with Eu-
calyptus spp. 
1.4.2 Location and Limits of the CCMP 
1.4.2.1 Spatial Limits 
The CCMP takes place in the Fortín Paunero Establishment, which is located in a rural 
area in the Guaminí department , northwest of the Buenos Aires province, Argentina  
(Figure 1). This region is known as the Pampean Plain , which is the most intensively 
modified region of the country . Once covered by native grasslands, it is now almost 
fully covered by agricultural lands and artificial grasslands, so it has practically no tree 
cover (Pereyra, 2012). 
The total area of the property where the CCMP is implemented is of 2.410 hec-
tares, from which 99,92 ha were selected for the implementation of the CCMP 1. As 
stated in section 2.3 Eligibility, the total area of the project matches eligibility require-
ments. In this sense, the total area of the project matches the eligible area. According 
to Cercarbono’s definitions as outlined in the Guidelines for Mapping Presentation and 
Analysis: 
• Total area: “This area encompasses the total area of a given program or 
project, including eligible and ineligible areas (which also include, where 
applicable, leakage monitoring areas considered by some programs or 
projects in the land use sector). Therefore, holders and developers shall 
generate the cartographic survey and present it as one or more poly-
gons, in which those areas are clearly identified” (p. 8). The total area of 
this CCMP consists of 99,92 hectares where the project activities will 
be implemented. 
• Eligible area: “It is the land surface, where the program or project certi-
fiable activities are carried out” (p. 8). The eligible area is made up of a 
reforestation segment consisting of 7 neighbouring lots that add 95,41 
ha, and a surface  for access roads and fire breaks that adds 4,51 ha . 
The reforestation segment and the roads and fire breaks add up 99,92 
ha, consistent with the total eligible area and the total project area. 
The rest of the property has historically been used for cattle ranching and ag-
riculture. 1.000 hectares are used for cattle ranching  and are covered with weeping 
lovegrass (Eragrostris curvula), which was planted before the current owners took 
over the property. Additionally, millet, corn, sunflower, wheat, soy, and barley are pro-
duced in different lots of the property. 
 
1 Geospatial files  complying with Guidelines for Mapping Presentation and Analysis  can be 
found in Supplementary Documentation folder 04.- Geospatial Files.

1.4.2.2 Time Limits 
The duration of the CCMP is of 30 years, from 2024.09.21 to 21.09. 2054.09.21. The 
first accreditation period is of 20 years, from 2024.09.21 to 2044.09.21. Initially, veri-
fications are estimated to take place every three years. 
1.4.2.3 CCMP Total Area 
The total area where the CCMP will produce climate change mitigation results through 
its reforestation segment is of 95,41 ha, which will be planted with Eucalyptus spp. 
This surface does not include the roads to access the different lots, only the lots 
themselves. The CCMP total area, including these roads, is of 99,92 ha. 
1.5  Hold ership or Right to  Use the Area  
The project takes place in one private property known as Fortín Paunero  Establish-
ment. This property is entirely owned by a family company called EFP S.A.2 The prop-
erty has been in the family since 1899, when it was bought directly from the Buenos 
Aires provincial government. Officially, it has been owned by EFP since 1978. 
 
2 Evidence of holdership  or property rights  can be found in Supplementary Documentation  
folder 02.-Holdership and Domain Rights.

Project Description Document for CCMP in the Land Use Sector   8 
 
1.6  Characteristics and Conditions Before the Start of 
the CCMP  
The previous conditions to the start of the CCMP are those of land that has been used 
for cattle ranching and agriculture for decades. Most of the reforestation segment was 
covered with weeping lovegrass (Eragostris curvula) that was used to feed cattle, and 
approximately 21,6 hectares have been used for agriculture. The last time a crop was 
produced in the project area was two years ago, when alfalfa (Medicago sativa) was 
grown on this surface. The baseline scenario is the same as the conditions before the 
start of the CCMP, so more detail can be found in section 0 Eligibility. 
1.6.1 Environmental Conditions 
The Fortín Paunero Establishment is situated in the southwest of Buenos Aires Prov-
ince, Argentina, in the Sandy Pampa subregion, spanning 2,333 hectares. This semi-
arid region experiences an average annual temperature of 14°C and receives around 
800 mm of rain annually, while potential evapotranspiration reaches 1,200 mm, result-
ing in a negative water balance (Oyarzabal et al., 2018). The area’s natural vegetation 
consists primarily of steppe and pseudo-steppe grasslands, along with various other 
types such as shrubs and rush beds, dominated by genera like Stipa, Poa, and Bromus 
(Oyarzabal et al. , 2018). Human activity, mainly agricultural expansion, has signifi-
cantly altered the natural environment. Agriculture, mixed farming, and livestock farm-
ing are the primary land uses  (Diaz Zorita et al. 2002, Hall et al., 1992), with summer 
crops prevailing in sandy plain areas and winter crops more uniformly distributed 
across the region (Marini et al., 2007). Forestry is not a common practice in this area 
(Lupi et al., 2013).

Half of the unit's surface consists of Class III soils (suitable for agriculture and for-
estry), and the other half is Class VI soils (moderately to marginally suitable for for-
estry). The Bolívar Series features sandy loam surface textures, non -alkaline, non-
saline, deep, and poorly developed soils found in a sandhill landscape. These soils 
have somewhat excessive to well-drained conditions, moderate to fast permeability, 
and medium runoff, with no flood risk and a deep-water table. The Veinticinco de 
Mayo Series, which covers 30% of the area, consists of deep, poorly developed soils 
suited for livestock, located on sandy ridges. This soil has excessive drainage, non -
alkaline, non-saline, but with limitations due to low nutrient supply, low moisture re-
tention, and susceptibility to wind erosion. Lastly, the Pirovano Series occupies gently 
undulating sandhills. These soils are deep, excessively drained, and contain 14% so-
dium alkalinity from 70 cm depth. These soils face challenges with moisture retention 
and wind erosion, though they have a richer organic matter content in the deeper 
horizons. 
 The scale of INTA’s information does not allow to identify the distribution of the 
different series that make up the CU. However, given the landowner’s description of 
the soil in the project area, emphasizing that it is very sandy and unsuitable for agri-
culture, one can assume that the series located in the project area might be a combi-
nation of Veinticinco de Mayo or Pirovano series.  The project's area is dominated by 
coarse-textured soils, resulting in lower water retention and reduced access to water 
for crops. These soils also feature high rainfall infiltration and excessive drainage, with 
low to medium surface runoff, reducing the risk of water erosion. Overall, they are 
low-fertility soils, making it difficult to stabilize and retain organic carbon. Their quality 
and productivity largely depend on organic matter inputs and management practices 
applied to them. 
1.6.3 Species Selection 
Several studies have assessed the forestry potential of the land in the Pampean Re-
gion. Moschini et al. (2000) evaluated the climatic suitability of various Eucalyptus 
species in Buenos Aires, creating a Climatic Suitability Index. They found that Euca-
lyptus viminalis is highly adaptable to the study region due to its resilience to frost and 
drought, making it well -suited for local climatic conditions. Additionally, Lupi et al.  
(2013) pointed out the potential of the Guaminí District, where Fortín Paunero i s lo-
cated, for forestry plantations aimed at carbon sequestration. F inally, the Food and 
Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (2020) further assessed the suitability 
of the land for E. viminalis plantations, particularly for energy production, finding it to 
be moderately suitable, although soils with Class III capability were excluded from this 
evaluation, despite being rated as very suitable for this species. 
E. viminalis has been shown to outperform E. camaldulensis in terms of annual 
growth. The former is expected to grow between 20 and 30 m³/ha/year depending on 
soil quality. However, it is sensitive to waterlogging and alkalinity, meaning it should 
be avoided in poorly drained areas. Given the soil characteristics of this CCMP, and 
the fact that there already are two E. viminalis 25-year-old plantations in the same 
property, we believe it is the species with the best characteristics to establish and 
develop correctly. Finally, more information regarding the two different eucalypt spe-
cies that are being tested in a small surface of the reforestation segment can be found 
in the following section.

In this case, the species to be established are eucalypts, which are per-

established a breeding program in 1995 to accommodate the growing demand

Nevertheless, no further attempts were made to plant more crops due to the soil’s 
characteristics, which do not favour their establishment13. Taking EFP S.A.’s traditional 
activities into account, it is important to emphasize that without th is CCMP, the land 
would remain with no forest cover as they would have no incentives to implement an 
afforestation14. 
Since this CCMP only includes one reforestation segment  to be implemented 
on heterogenous agricultural lands without woody crops15, the carbon pools that apply 
for this estimation are aboveground and belowground tree biomass. Regarding emis-
sion sources, according to the methodology, fires are conservatively excluded in the 
baseline scenario. Additionally, emissions from fertiliser use and fossil fuel consump-
tion in agricultural machinery can only be considered in woody crops segments, so 
they are not included in this CCMP baseline scenario. With regards to emissions from 
burning, no burning activities have been implemented by EFP S.A. in any of their agri-
cultural practices, so they are accounted for as zero. 
It is important to note that, while some information regarding the baseline sce-
nario comes from official government sources, some also comes from questionnaires 
applied to the landowners (EFP S.A.) throughout several meetings. Whenever any ev-
idence was available for sharing, it was included as supplementary documentation. 
While we consider this CCMP to be constructed on reliable information, this limitation 
has to be considered.

Species Selection and Seedling Sourcing 
On one hand, Eucalyptus viminalis was chosen as the main species for the afforesta-
tion. This decision was based on visits to the project area and a literature review (Mos-
chini et al., 2000; Lupi et al., 2013; Food and Agriculture Organization, 2020), conclud-
ing that it is one of the species best adapted to the climatic conditions of the Pampean 
Region16. On the other hand, Garruchos S.A. was interested in testing two other euca-
lypt species to see which ones could have a good development. According to previous 
tests run by Garruchos  S.A., E. camaldulensis usually has a certain tolerance to low 
temperatures and good growth, which means it may have potential in the project area. 
The second species, E. grandis, is a slightly riskier bet. It was selected for its good 
growth and health in the province of Corrientes, where most of their operations are 
located. Additionally, this species occasionally showed tolerance to low temperatures 
if they are not extreme. Hence, this last species was planted in a very small test sur-
face to evaluate its performance. In total, the surface planted with these three mate-
rials is of 0,29 ha. 
 All the seedlings were produced in the Garruchos S.A. nursery in the province 
of Corrientes, located in Ituzaingó. Garruchos S.A. has more than 20 years of experi-
ence in seedling production, and the nursery has a production capacity of 6 million 
seedlings per year. The seedlings underwent a hardening process, during which they 
were exposed to direct sunlight for at least a month, thus leaving the controlled con-
ditions of the nursery and acclimating to uncontrolled conditions. During this process, 
the seedlings produce more lignin, which hardens their trunks and prepares them  to 
go out into the field. Thus, to leave the nursery, they have the following characteris-
tics: 
• Height of 20 to 30 cm 
• Undergone at least a month of direct sunlight for the hardening process 
• Abundant root system, with many white roots (indicating that they are active) 
Site Selection 
The site for the implementation of the reforestation segment of this CCMP was se-
lected together with EFP.  As owners of the property, which focuses on agricultural 
production, EFP wanted to implement the project in an area where only livestock farm-
ing was carried out because carbon removal projects can hardly compete with the 
profitability of agricultural activities.  This way, it was decided to use a sector of the 
property where agricultural activities had failed to succeed and where an E. viminalis 
plantation was more likely to develop correctly. In Figure 9, it can be noted that the 
CCMP total area lies between two patches of forest, which correspond to 25-years-
old E. viminalis plantations. These were planted with intentions of producing cellulose 
for the paper industry, but were finally left untouched.

Fencing / Reforestation Segment Protection 
The total CCMP area was already fenced, as it used to be a ranching area surrounded 
by agricultural lands . The fence is made of wooden poles and smooth and barbed 
wire. Garruchos S.A.’s team verified the state of the entire perimeter before the start 
of the land preparation.  It is important to note that the intrusion of cattle is unlikely  
because most of the surrounding plots are used for agriculture. 
Land Preparation 
Most of the land was prepared with a Northeast-Southwest orientation, drawing par-
allel lines to the fence that marks the limit of the EFP property. There are approxi-
mately 7 hectares that have an East-West orientation. Before this activity began, Gar-
ruchos S.A.’s team verified that the soil was at field capacity17 to prevent soil erosion. 
Land preparation consisted in the subsoiling of the plantation lines, which were drilled 
with a spike to a depth of approximately 60 cm  (and not less than 45 cm),  without 
removing the soil (Figure 10 A). The purpose of this activity was to aerate the soil’s 
superficial profiles where the tree roots will develop, helping them to grow optimally.

Right behind the tractor’s subsoiling discs, came different discs that created a furrow 
in the plantation strip. This furrow is concave (Figure 10 B), allowing water to accumu-

portant part of the land preparation process because these soils are very sandy. This 
land preparation process for the reforestation segment resulted in tree lines with an 8

Planting 
Eucalypt plantations are carried out in autumn or spring. Ideally, spring is preferred, 
so that the seedlings have several months of medium and high temperatures to es-
tablish and correctly develop their root system and good bearing. For this CCMP, the 
plantation design is 8 meters between rows and 2 meters between plants, with an 
initial density of 625 trees per hectare. After thinning, which will have an intensity of 
50%, there will be 312 plants per hectare. 
An initial control of weeds and pests was carried out, so that the planting strips 
were free of weeds and ants. Then, the actual planting was done manually (Figure 11 
A), ensuring that the planting depth was up to the level of the seedling's neck and 
gently tamping the soil around it to avoid the creation of air bubbles in the root zone 
(Figure 11 B). Seedlings were planted with the help of a planting spike in biodegradable 
containers made of paper. As mentioned earlier, the plantation design is 8 meters be-
tween rows and 2 meters between plants, resulting in an initial density of 625 trees 
per hectare.

Fertilization 
Immediately after planting, each plant was supplied with 80 gr of N-P-K Diammonium 
Phosphate. Fertilizer application was done through two holes 15 or 20 cm away from 
the plant, where the product was deposited and then covered with soil. This step was 
done carefully to avoid the dispersion of fertilizer.  
Weeds & Pests Control 
In order to help combat weed germination, a pre-emergent was applied on the plant-
ing strips of the reforestation segment after the planting activities concluded . The 
ideal dose is 0,15 kg per hectare, achieved after the calibration of the application

Regarding pests, the most common in eucalypt plantations in Argentina  are 
leafcutter ants. These have not yet been observed in the project area, but when they 
are, Garruchos S.A. will proceed as follows. Ant controls are exclusively carried out 
with products permitted by the National Service for Health and Food Quality (SENASA 
in Spanish) and by the Forest Stewardship Council (FSC)18. It is important to note that 
Garruchos S.A. is committed to use a minimum amount of these products, as well as 
to substitute them for alternatives with a lower socio-environmental impact whenever 
feasible. 
 Granulated bait made of a citrus pulp attractant and a non -volatile active in-
gredient with a low concentration of sulfluramid or fipronil is used. The product is sen-
sitive to climate and humidity, therefore, there should not be much humidity in the soil 
at the time of application. In the case of Atta ants, 10 g of product per square meter 
of anthill must be applied on the sides of the haul lanes. And in the case of Acro ants, 
a maximum of 30 g per square meter of anthill must be applied in the same manner19. 
If the dose applied to the anthill is insufficient, the ants identify the threat. They 
receive an alarm that the nests are being poisoned, they close, isolate, and cut them 
off, and take the queen somewhere else. They lower their activity for 10 days and then 
reactivate and continue as if nothing happened. The ants that remained alive can rec-
ognize the product. Therefore, a waiting period of 90 days must occur before a sec-
ond application in order to wait for them to die (new generations no longer recognize 
it).

ally, replacing the few seedlings that did not establish in order to maintain the initial

with a chainsaw. The loading onto the truck is carried  out with a loading ma-
chine. 
• Manual: In the case of manual felling, safety and protection must be prioritized. 
The personnel must be properly trained and qualified. In this system, the pro-
cess begins with the felling of the trees and their subsequent delimbing within 
the stand using a chain saw. Then, the logs are extracted from the roadside 
using a mini skidder or modified agricultural tractor. At this point, an operator 
measures and classifies the rolls, followed by cutting them with a chainsaw . 
Finally, they are loaded onto the truck using a loading machine.

3 Quantification of GHG Emissions and Removals 
3.1 Quantification of GHG Emissions and Removals in the B aseline 
Scenario    
As described in section 2.7 GHG Emission Sources, the baseline scenario’s emissions 
can be accounted for as zero. Regarding removals, according to the CDM A/R Tool 14, 
carbon stock in trees can be accounted as zero in the baseline scenario if the following 
three conditions are met: 
a) The pre-project trees are neither harvested, nor cleared, nor removed through-
out the crediting period of the project activity; 
b) The pre-project trees do not suffer mortality because of competition from trees 
planted in the project, or damage because of implementation of the project 
activity, at any time during the crediting period of the project activity; 
c) The pre-project trees are not inventoried along with the project trees in moni-
toring of carbon stocks but their continued existence, consistent with the 
baseline scenario, is monitored throughout the crediting period of the project 
activity (CDM A/R Tool 14, p. 6). 
Since the baseline scenario consist of heterogenous agricultural lands without woody 
crops, with no trees on entire surface of the reforestation segment, there are no pre-
project trees (Figure 12). Hence, no pre-project trees are harvested, nor cleared nor 
removed, nor suffer mortality rate, nor are inventoried along with the project trees. 
So, in conclusion, the baseline above and belowground tree biomass can be ac-
counted for as zero.

3.3 Leakage  
As justified in section 0 GHG Emission Sources , no leakage due to displacement of 
agricultural activities is taken into account in this CCMP. According to the methodol-
ogy, leakages should be estimated using  the AR-TOOL15 –A/R Methodological tool: 
Estimation of the increase in GHG emissions attributable to displacement of pre pro-
ject agricultural activities in A/R CDM project activity (version 02.0). This tool indicates 
that leakage can be considered insignificant under the following conditions: 
- Animals are displaced to existing grazing lands and the total number of animals 
does not exceed the load capacity of this land 
- Animals are displaced to zero grazing systems, like the sale of meat. 
Hence, as the displaced animals were sold for meat 28, it is possible to consider that 
there is no leakage to be accounted for in this CCMP  in regards of animal displace-
ment. 
3.4 Net GHG Removals  
As per the methodology, the ex-ante net GHG benefits from this CCMP29 were esti-
mated by balancing the baseline with the project emissions and the gross removals 
due to the modelled growth of the eucalypt afforestation. In this sense, the estimation 
is that this CCMP will be able to remove a total of 74.706 tCO2e throughout its life-
time30 (Table 6). It is important to highlight that , prior to every verification event, a 
portion of the Carboncers generated will be destined to the project’s buffer. The per-
centage of credits destined for the pooled buffer is of 5%, while the individual buffer 
may vary from verification to verification and is currently estimated to be 6,3%, as 
detailed in section 7 Risks, Uncertainty, and Non -Permanence and in 2022.08.10 -

4.2 Link with NDCs  
Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) form the foundation for countries that 
signed and ratified the Paris Agreement and a part of the United Nations Framework 
Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) to meet its goals regarding climate change 
mitigation and adaptation. Each participating nation is required to update and report 
on its targets, policies, and measures for reducing national emissions and adapting to 
climate change, at least every five years.  In this sense, Argentina ’s National Climate 
Change Cabinet released the country's second NDC report in 2020 and updated it in 
2021 (United Nations Development Programme, n.d.). 
Taking into account that this PMCC aims to remove GHG emissions through 
ARR activities, the carbon credits that will be generated in the future are related to the 
country’s absolute goal, which is to not exceed a net total of 349 million tCO2e in 2030 
(MAyDS, 2020). The National Strategy for the Use of Carbon Markets (MAyDS, 2023), 
which was published in 2023, states that in line with Argentina's Second NDC (2020), 
any activity involving mitigation results achieved within Argentine territory, whether 
by public or private entities, must be registered and explicitly authorized by the  na-
tional government. Unless specified otherwise, all mitigation results will be accounted 
for in meeting Argentina’s NDC targets under the Paris Agreemen t’s Article 6, which 
governs voluntary cooperation mechanisms. 
The PMCC will be properly registered (the procedure is outlined in the supple-
mentary document Normogram, found in folder 0 6.- Legal Requirements. However, 
the National Strategy has not been translated into laws that indicate which govern-
ment body is responsible for emitting the authorizations and approvals, so this part is 
yet to be enforced. It is worth noting that during the current administration, the former 
Ministry for Environment and Sustainable Development was downgraded and trans-
formed into an Undersecretariat, which was fused with Sports and Tourism in the Sec-
retariat for Tourism, Environment, and Sports 35. This reflects the position of the cur-
rent administration regarding environmental and climate adaptation issues, making it 
clear that it is not a priority to further develop the country’s National Strategy for the 
use of Carbon Markets. However, a ny updates will be reported in the following

formity and corresponding corrective actions will be carried out within a reasonable 
time period.

section 0 Carbon Pools, this will be carried out through a forest inventory, where the 
entire project area will be classified into strata. Within each stratum, cartographic soft-
ware will be used to determine the random distribution of permanent circular plots, 
where all the trees will be measured as described below . For intermediate years

Sampling Plan 
The field measurements will be conducted based on predefined statistical parameters 
to ensure precision and confidence in the results. The methodology for conducting 
the inventory will follow th is Monitoring and Quality Management Plan  and include 
determining the following variables: 
• Sample size 
• Sampling error 
• Sampling process 
• Mapping of sample locations 
• Field data collection (including measured variables and the instruments used) 
• Calculation methods 
• Statistical analysis 
The project boundaries will be established at the start of the project and updated as 
necessary throughout the crediting period, remaining within the initially validated area. 
In the event of unplanned contingencies such as fires, droughts, or pests, new strata 
may be created, and boundaries may be adjusted accordingly.  Geographic coordi-
nates are determined, documented, and stored. A Geographic Information System 
(GIS) will be utilized, following the Guidelines for Mapping Presentation and Analysis. 
The population under study is generally uniform in terms of species types and 
combinations, planting densities, planting years, topography, and soil types, with only 
one lot differing in species composition. To address this variation, the population is

divided into strata to improve precision and reduce variability in the variables influ-
encing carbon stock changes above and below ground. Stratification helps eliminate 
variability that could obscure inventory results, ensuring that within-stratum variability 
is lower than that of the overall population. This approach also enhances the accuracy 
of estimations and simplifies data collection, processing, and fieldwork planning. 
Since species composition is the only variable that differs, it was the sole factor 
used to define the strata, resulting in the creation of two strata , both of which are 
mapped and identified in the Geographic Information System (GIS): 
• Stratum 1: Eucalyptus viminalis 
• Stratum 2: Eucalyptus spp 
The sampling design establishes the variables to be used, including plot distribution, 
quantity, sizes, and data analysis techniques. A "Systematic Random" design was 
chosen, employing a rectangular grid to locate plots within each stratum. The plots 
are distributed across the area of interest in homogeneous units (lots) to determine 
the dasometric parameters representing these lots. Permanent sampling plots are 
used to measure and monitor carbon stock changes over time, as they are more ef-
fective at reducing variance caused by plot effects. 
For plot placement, QGIS tools are utilized. A 15-meter perimeter buffer is cre-
ated around each polygon to avoid placing plots near polygon boundaries. Plots are 
randomly located for the first sampling, ensuring each polygon contains at least one 
plot based on its surface area. The exact locations are determined using GPS. The 
sample size, defined by the number of plots in each stratum, is based on statistical 
criteria to achieve the desired accuracy and precision levels. Plot size balances accu-
racy, precision, and cost-efficiency, and must accommodate an adequate number of 
trees for measurement. Following IPCC Good Practice Guidance for LULUCF, Chapter 
4.3, which recommends plot sizes between 100 m² and 600 m² depending on tree 
density, circular plots of 400 m² have been selected to monitor the strata, considering 
the project's specific conditions. 
Permanent sampling plots are utilized to monitor and evaluate changes in carbon 
stocks over time for the most significant carbon pools. These plots are designed to 
minimize variance from plot effects, improving the accuracy of carbon stock esti-
mates. Located with GPS and discreetly marked, they are made as inconspicuous as 
possible to prevent special treatments (e.g., during soil preparation, weeding, fertili-
zation, or harvesting) that might impact tree growth. The plots are also safeguarded 
against deforestation throughout the crediting period. 
The initial number of sampling plots was calculated using the Calculation of the 
number of sample plots for measurements within A/R CDM project activities tool, re-
sulting in 97 plots for the entire project area. This was later adjusted to 100 plots, with 
the number of circular plots per stratum determined proportionally to the stratum’s 
area. To maintain statistical independence, a minimum of two plots per stratum was 
ensured, and any strata with fewer plots were adjusted accordingly to meet t his re-
quirement, achieving a 10% significance level. Measurements will occur every three 
years, with a designated area of Garruchos S.A. overseeing th e coordination. Data 
collection will be outsourced to a specialized service provider, with results reviewed 
by Garruchos S.A. to ensure accuracy and consistency.

The materials needed for the field measurements are: field maps, field sheets, 
plastic/aluminum labels, spray paint (ideally orange or yellow) , colored plastic tapes, 
permanent markers, wooden stakes, machete, first aid kit, security equipment, GPS, 
Vertex67, telescopic rod, diametric tape, and forceps. During the field measurements, 
a GPS will be used to locate the center of the sampling plots. The CCMP area has 
good satellite reception, so there is no risk of locating the plots incorrectly. To locate 
the plot center, the operator will navigate with the GPS until the planned waypoint is 
found and wait until the margin of error of the satellite location is 2 meters or less. 
Then the center of the plot is determined in such a way that it is in the middle of 4 
surrounding trees. A cairn or rustic stake will be installed, and all the perimeter trees 
will be marked with paint. 
Each pool will be measured following all methodology and protocol requirements, 
as well as IPCC Good Practice Guidance for LULUCF (Penman, 2003) and the corre-
sponding SOP68. Measurements of biometric variables will be conducted every three 
years on a predetermined date, ideally around the same time each year. While winter 
is considered an optimal season for these measurements due to the physiological dor-
mancy of trees and improved accessibility, other factors such as planting schedules, 
logistical considerations, and verification timelines should also be evaluated when de-
termining the timing of measurements. 
• Diameter at breast height (DBH):  All diameters will be measured at 1,30 m 
above ground level, with diametric tape or a forceps, according to the size of 
the tree. Stems with a DBH larger than 2 cm will be included in the measure-
ment, and individuals with less than 1,30 m of height will not be included in the 
inventory. 
• Height: Tree height, defined as the linear distance along its main axis from the 
ground to the apex or a specific reference point. This measurement is crucial 
for calculating both volume and height increments. For carbon credit monitor-
ing, the total height will be  recorded. To measure trees larger than 4 m , the 
base of the tree is first cleared of weeds and debris. The operator then posi-
tions themselves at a distance of at least twice the height of the tree. After 
activating the Vertex, a laser beam is used to assist in measurements. By 
pressing the trigonometry key three times, the operator aligns the laser pointer 
with the base of the tree and then gradually raises it to the apex. If visibility of 
the apex is obstructed, the zoom feat ure (1x, 2x, or 4x) can be utilized to im-
prove accuracy. A telescopic rod is used for trees smaller than 4 m. 
The operator will begin by measuring the row furthest to the left in relation to the 
plot's access road, progressing along the row to its end and then returning in the 
opposite direction, continuing this pattern. The first tree will be marked with the 
number 1 using paint, and all measured trees will receive a spray mark at 1.3 meters 
height. The procedure involves measuring all trees with a Diameter at Breast 
Height (DBH) of 2 cm or more, starting from the north radius of the plot and moving 
clockwise.
